# Jāliya Sutta (DN 7 (PTS DN i 159))

**ID:** DN 7 (PTS DN i 159)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Jāliya Sutta* is the seventh text of the *Dīghanikāya* and belongs to its opening division, the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* [Hazra 1994; Norman 1983]. Set at the Ghositārāma monastery in Kosambī, the discourse records a visit by two wandering ascetics (*paribbājaka*s)—Mandissa and Jāliya, a pupil of the wooden-bowl ascetics (*dārupattika*)—who ask whether the soul or life principle (*jīva*) is identical with or distinct from the physical body (*sarīra*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Dhammika; Jennings 1948; Walshe 1987]. Rather than treating this unresolved metaphysical question directly, the Buddha details the sequence of spiritual training established in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2)—advancing through moral restraint (*sīla*), the meditative absorptions, and liberating knowledge—arguing that one who has realized higher insight and arahantship no longer entertains such speculative dichotomies [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Gyatso 1992; Hazra 1994; Norman 1983; Walshe 1987].

The text is largely identical to the concluding portion of the immediately preceding *Mahāli Sutta* (DN 6), where the exchange with Jāliya is quoted by the Buddha as an earlier event [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Walshe 1987]. Modern scholars have noted that the *Jāliya Sutta* was likely incorporated into DN 6 prior to the final redaction of the *Dīghanikāya*, since the discussion of *sīla* occurs only within the Jāliya portion, thereby providing the justification for DN 6's placement in the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983]. Govind Chandra Pande observes that the text veers abruptly into a standard recapitulation of the *Sāmaññaphala* path, suggesting that its original framing conclusion may have been lost [Kingsbury 2002; Pande 1974].

Neither the *Jāliya Sutta* nor the *Mahāli Sutta* survives as an independent discourse in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (T 1) [Banerjee 1979; Kingsbury 2002; Pande 1974]. SuttaCentral lists full and partial parallels with Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta 19) and numerous Nikāya discourses sharing the gradual training formulas [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies 750 Pali-internal reuse passages across 60 canonical texts, primarily sharing nearly its entire text with DN 6 (§1.3–5.11 ↔ §15.2–19.11) as well as significant sections with the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta* (DN 9) and *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignment, DharmaNexus identifies a match with the Chinese *Xiéjiàn jīng* (T 93) [DharmaNexus]. Canonical reference to the text is also found in the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 14) and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 10.3, Kv 18.9) [SuttaCentral].
